title: local Variables
summary: `local` declares a variable that only exists inside the block where it was created. It is faster and safer than globals — in Roblox code, nearly every variable should be local.

syntax: local a, b = 1, 2            -- multiple locals at once
local name                   -- declares first, assigns later

details.heading: Scope and lifetime
details.body: A local is visible from its declaration until the end of the enclosing block — a block is the body of a function, an `if`/`for`/`while`/`do` statement, or the whole script. When the block ends, the local can no longer be accessed.

details.heading: Performance
details.body: Locals are stored in fast VM registers; globals go through a table lookup in `_G`. Tight loops using locals can be noticeably faster than global lookups.

explanation.whatItIs: `local` creates a variable whose lifetime and visibility are limited to the block it was declared in. Write `local coins = 50` inside a function, and nothing outside that function can see `coins`.
explanation.whyItExists: Locals prevent name collisions, make code easier to reason about (the value can only change inside the block you're reading), keep memory tidy, and run faster than globals.
whenToUse: For essentially every variable you write: `local`, then the name
Inside loops and callbacks, to avoid leaking names outward
At the top of a script, to cache services: `local Players = game:GetService("Players")`
whenNotToUse: Almost never omit it. The only common intentional global is shared state like `_G.something`, and even that is better done with ModuleScripts or attributes
explanation.mentalModel:
```text
do
    local secret = 42
    print(secret)   --> 42
end
print(secret)       --> nil  (out of scope)
```
Each `do ... end`, function, loop, or `if` body is a room. A `local` is born in that room and dies when you leave it.
tips: If the autocomplete/underline says a variable is global, you probably forgot `local`
Declare at the top of the scope where it is used, not pages earlier
Closures can capture locals — see the closures entry
commonMistakes: Declaring `local x` inside an `if` block and then trying to read `x` after the `end`
Re-declaring with `local` by accident inside a loop: `local count = count + 1` makes a *new* local each iteration instead of updating the outer one
Assuming `local` makes a value unchangeable — it does not. There is no const in Luau

examples.title: Scope in action
examples.code:
local outside = "I live in the whole script"

if true then
    local inside = "I only live in this if block"
    print(inside)   --> works
    print(outside)  --> works (outer locals are visible inside)
end

print(outside)      --> works
print(inside)       --> nil! `inside` no longer exists
examples.commonMistake: Beginners often declare a variable inside an `if`/`for` block and are surprised when it's nil afterwards. Declare it *before* the block if you need it after.

examples.title: The accidental re-declaration bug
examples.code:
local total = 0
for i = 1, 5 do
    local total = total + i   -- BUG: new local, shadows outer one
end
print(total)                  --> still 0!

-- Correct:
local sum = 0
for i = 1, 5 do
    sum = sum + i             -- no `local` here: updates the outer one
end
print(sum)                    --> 15
examples.whyItWorks: Inside the loop, `local total` creates a fresh variable that shadows the outer one each iteration, so the outer `total` is never touched.
examples.commonMistake: Adding `local` when you meant to update an existing variable. Only the *first* declaration gets `local`.
